text:
A dispute between the Portland Hearings Office and the landlord of the building that houses Portland's ICE facility will likely remain tied up in Multnomah County Circuit Court until at least the fall.

The court agreed to review a land-use violation the city of Portland issued to building owner Stuart Lindquist after his lawyers argued that the Portland hearings officer who denied Lindquist's appeal could not impartially review the case.

Lindquist's lawyers claim that hearings officer Charles Koutras rescheduled a hearing on the appeal because of outside safety concerns affecting hearings officers. They argue that Koutras' decision to reschedule the hearing from a date previously agreed upon by Lindquist and the city attorney demonstrates that he is not impartial.

"Isolated but significant security incidents implicating the safety of Hearings Officers and clerks have highlighted the need for the Hearings Office to complete its review of this case and issue a decision as efficiently as possible," Koutras' rescheduling order reads, in part.

READ ALSO | Lawsuit seeks to compel feds to release ICE detention center plans for Oregon

The city's Hearings Office has declined to comment on the case or provide further details about the alleged safety issue.

The Multnomah County judge overseeing the case agreed to pause all consequences stemming from the land-use violation, including fines, while the court reviews the case.

A hearing scheduled for Friday, during which the city was set to submit the record of its land-use violation case against Lindquist, was postponed. Lindquist's lawyers said they agreed to extend the city's deadline to submit the record until Sept. 11 and expect the court to schedule a hearing sometime in November.

The city issued the land-use violation notice Sept. 18 following complaints from some Portland residents. The notice alleges Lindquist's tenant, the Department of Homeland Security, is violating conditions the city imposed when it approved the building for use as a temporary ICE holding facility in 2011.

The city alleges the tenant is violating those conditions by covering the building's glass windows with wooden boards and holding detainees at the facility for more than 12 hours.

Lindquist's lawyers argue that the wooden boards are a temporary measure installed in response to "violent" protesters.

"The alleged violation for protective window boarding without design review improperly presumes that window boarding is a permanent change to the façade. It is not permanent, but is only deployed so long as necessary to protect the building from well documented violence," documents filed in court by Lindquist's lawyers read.

His lawyers also dispute the city's assertion that the building's original approval conditions prohibit detainees from being held there for 12 hours or longer.

Lindquist's lawyers declined to comment on the pending case.

An immigration advocacy group called Portland Contra Las Deportaciones has been calling and messaging city leaders in an effort to move the case forward and begin enforcement of the land-use violation fines. The group had planned to gather outside the courthouse Friday ahead of the hearing but canceled the gathering after the hearing was postponed.

Cami Saunders, an organizer for the group, said its members were not involved in any alleged safety issues or threats against the hearings officer.

"We had no communications with the hearings officer and, as far as I am concerned, we have been the primary group pushing for the revocation of the permit and for this hearings process to move along. I know that we have put lots of pressure on city officials, like the city council and this hearings officer, like, we wanted them to uphold the land-use violation, but no threats were made by us," she said.

text:
Haitians living in Springfield, Ohio are being required to wear ankle monitors and turn their passports over to United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

Haitians in Springfield are getting letters telling them to report to the ICE office in either Blue Ash (near Cincinnati) or Westerville (near Columbus).

“When they do, their passports are collected,” said Carl Ruby, pastor of Springfield’s Central Christian Church.

“They’re fitted with ankle (monitors); I call them ankle shackles.”

This is happening after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in June that President Donald Trump can end temporary protected status for the 330,000 Haitians who’ve fled the violence in their home country.

TPS officially ended for Haitians on July 27 and a court lifted an injunction last week.

About 15,000 Haitians live in Springfield, with a mixture of temporary protected status, citizenship, and other legal status.

Even though about 30,000 Haitians with temporary status live in central Ohio, only Haitians in Springfield are being asked to wear the ankle monitors as of now, Ruby said.

“What you’re seeing in Ohio is a Springfield focused effort,” he said.

He has gone down to ICE’s Blue Ash office with some Haitians to receive their ankle monitors, which can track where people are at any given moment and have about a 75 mile radius, Ruby said.

“The ICE officers indicated, ‘If you keep coming back every time we call you, that may help your immigration case,’ which I don’t believe,” he said.

“I think it’s a means to round up people quickly, and that when they’re ready, they have the logistics in place to deport them. I think that’s what’s going to happen.”

The Haitians are then told to report back to the ICE office when they are summoned, which is expected to be every three to four weeks, Ruby said.

“It’s inciting a lot of fear,” Ruby said. “I think (ICE’s) real goal is for them to self-deport. … I think it boils down to they want to have complete control over them, so (ICE) can easily deport them as soon as they’re ready.”

Ruby is unaware of any Haitians from Springfield who have self-deported back to Haiti.

The U.S. Department of State currently has a Level 4 “Do Not Travel” advisory for Haiti “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited health care,” according to the state department. A top security official and chief of staff to the nation’s defense minister was kidnapped in June.

“It just makes me sick thinking of the sexual violence that is the norm in Haiti,” Ruby said. “There there are kids who sat next to our kids in Springfield City Schools who are going to be raped if they’re sent back, and that’s just the truth.”

More than 1,000 children born in Springfield with American citizenship have Haitian parents. Springfield City Schools declined to comment for the story.

ICE detained 35 people — including four Haitians — in central Ohio between Aug. 5 through Aug. 10, said Maqueli Eldredge, a paralegal at Legal Immigration Services in Dublin. Ruby said he has not noticed an increased ICE presence in Springfield.

“They say they would come for the Haitians on this special task force, but they take any collateral damage people,” Eldredge said in a text message.

The ICE office in Westerville was full of Haitians coming out with ankle monitors when Eldredge was there last week.

Many of their Brazilian clients in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia were asked to start wearing ankle monitors in July 2025. She said they have a 16-year-old client wearing an ankle monitor in Pittsburgh.

“It is very embarrassing to wear them,” Eldredge said in a text message. “(The) devices cause lesions, rashes and blisters, bleeding on their ankles.”

She said it can be hard for their clients to sleep with the ankle monitors.

“It beeps in the middle of the night and (it’s) hard to get comfortable,” Eldredge said in a text message.

The ankle monitors will start beeping if the battery is not functioning well, Eldredge said.

“They break all the time and batteries malfunction and get very hot, some caught on fire when charging,” she said in a text message.

Some people are afraid of going back to the ICE office, so Eldredge knows folks who have cut off the ankle monitors and leave the state or self-deport.

“(Officials) follow up where they leave that monitor and sometimes just take some collaterals,” she said.

text:
Steuben County Sheriff Allard reacts: The Steuben County Sheriff’s Office will follow and enforce all laws

By Andrew Harris

NY Governor Kathy Hochul and Attorney General Letitia James issued a joint statement this morning regarding legal mandate to end all 287g agreement with federal Immigration and Customs Enforcement(ICE.)

The statement indicates that of the twelve agencies notified to end the agreements, five have formally notified NYS that they will comply. The remaining seven agencies were reminded that they have just 11 days to “unwind” such agreements.

Here is the statement issued by the Governor and AG:

“Local police should be focused on one thing: keeping their communities safe. Since we notified the 12 law enforcement agencies with 287(g) agreements, five have told us they intend to comply with state law. The seven remaining agencies, including the Nassau County Sheriff’s Office and Police Department, have 11 days to formally unwind their agreements with ICE.

“The safety of New Yorkers is our top priority. That’s why New York passed these laws, why we will enforce them, and why we will continue standing up to federal overreach. Our job is to enforce the law, and that is exactly what we plan on doing.”

We asked Steuben County Sheriff James Allard for his reaction and any updates on how Steuben County will respond to the state. Allard suggested that his office and the county had no reason to “unwind” any agreement as the NYS law renders the 287g agreement currently in place null and void as of August 25th. The Sheriff echoed the sentiments of Steuben County leadership and the Public Safety Committee:

“Local police should be allowed to focus on local public safety, not forced to follow politically driven mandates from Albany. As the Governor makes statements about no county or agency being above the law, the NYS government consistently places themselves above federal law, picking and choosing which federal statute they will or will not follow, doing precisely what they are accusing local municipalities of doing. The Governor and the Attorney General both know that the Federal Government has a supremacy clause over state governments, but that counties have home rule in relation to their state government.

The Steuben County Sheriff’s Office will follow and enforce all laws. We will coordinate and cooperate with all local, state and federal law enforcement agencies. There is no section of the Executive Law which requires “unwinding” of contracts, whatever that may mean. The Executive Law as written makes all 287-g contracts null and void as of August 25th, 2026. Again, we will follow the law.

text:
LOS ANGELES — Corissa Hernandez still recalls how quickly business shifted at Nativo, her bar and restaurant in the Highland Park neighborhood, as federal immigration agents ramped up enforcement operations across the city last June and caused uncertainty among her staff and customers.

She wasn’t alone. A newly published report from the Latino Policy and Politics Institute at the University of California, Los Angeles suggests that there were colossal economic repercussions for small businesses across Los Angeles County, finding that establishments across nine enforcement sites experienced about 46,000 fewer visits and approximately $3.16 million in losses within two weeks of enforcement activities.

“It felt like a lot of us were very vigilant at the front door, and a lot of our community members and team were coming in here distressed, whether it was fear for their family, their friends,” Hernandez told MS NOW. She estimates that her sales dipped by as much as 40%, in part because potential customers were hesitant to leave their homes amid heightened Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in their communities.

Hernandez described the ICE raids as particularly frustrating considering how reliant the restaurant industry is on immigrant labor.

“Restaurants and bars cannot exist without immigrants,” she said. “It’s in every aspect of what we do, from the people who are out in the fields picking the food that we’re eating, to the people preparing our food, to the people serving it, to the people owning these spaces.”

Patrons have slowly returned for cocktails and fresh Mexican fare, and the World Cup gave her a much-needed boost. But still, Hernandez remains on edge.

“I can’t say that we’re 100% prepared,” she said. “I don’t think anyone ever is when something so traumatic happens, but we strive to ensure that we’re still maintaining as safe of a space as possible.”

The UCLA study also found that 95% of Latino business owners reported continued financial stress almost a year after Trump’s aggressive national crackdown began, a long-term impact that surprised the report’s lead author, Amada Armenta, also the director of the Latino Policy and Politics Institute.

“I think what became very clear was that there has just been a series of what our respondents called ‘disasters’ or ‘emergencies,’ from Covid to the fires to the ICE raids, and that not only did they feel like it was more difficult to recover [than] in the past, but also almost like their reserves had been exhausted,” Armenta told MS NOW. “So many people talked about draining their savings accounts to stay afloat, taking on additional business debt, and then I think what was most surprising to us was also the amount of emotional stress and health problems that people reported, chronic health conditions that used to be under control that were no longer under control.”

Additional research from business professor Exequiel Hernandez at the Wharton School suggests similar downturns could be playing out at shops nationwide. In his report, titled “ICE-ing the Economy: Immigration Enforcement Under Trump 2.0 and Local Economic Activity,” Hernandez analyzed foot-traffic and spending data for 5.4 million businesses across the country between January 2024 and February 2026; he found 8.1 billion fewer visits to businesses and as much as a $14 billion decrease in retail spending across metropolitan areas targeted by federal immigration enforcement operations.

In Los Angeles’ Fashion District, where federal agents raided a clothing business last June, City Council member Ysabel Jurado says vendors are still struggling to rebuild both their businesses and their sense of safety.

“During the Fourth of July weekend that year, one of the vendors said they only made $3 the whole weekend, and that Fourth of July weekend is usually when they would make so much money that would last them the summer, and now they’re trying to subsist out of $3,” Jurado said. “How is that going to be sustainable for anybody? And so, it was just so devastating. And recovering from that is something that’s going to take years to do.”

Jurado compared Los Angeles’ ICE raids to a period of martial law in the Philippines that drove her parents to flee to the United States.

“I live at home with my dad, and I was just thinking about the irony of the fact that that was what my parents left, and now it’s at my doorstep as the first time ever being a council member, and I think within the first six months of my tenure,” she said.

Asked about the economic impact of immigration enforcement activity on Latino-owned small businesses, a Department of Homeland Security spokesperson told MS NOW, “Let’s be clear, if there was any correlation between rampant illegal immigration and a good economy, [Joe] Biden would have had a booming economy. Removing these criminals from the streets makes communities safer for business owners and customers.”

The spokesperson also touted the administration’s deportation totals.

Recommended

“In President Trump’s first year back in office, more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the U.S. because of the Trump administration’s crackdown on illegal immigration including an estimated 2.2 million self-deportations. As of Aug. 4, we have now deported over 1 million illegal aliens and arrested over 1 million illegal aliens.”

In Highland Park, a neighborhood dotted with restaurants and coffee shops, City Council member Eunisses Hernandez painted a different picture of the community she grew up in, which she says is still on its toes more than a year after the initial surge.

“They’re not going after the worst of the worst. That is a distraction,” Eunisses Hernandez said. “They’re going after anybody that looks brown. That’s what we’ve seen in our district. That’s what we’ve seen in this city.”

As the businesses in her district work to recover, Eunisses Hernandez said the enforcement activity was enough to push some already struggling local shops over the edge.

“What we’ve also seen is that many of the businesses that have been impacted by the federal immigration raids haven’t been able to open up again,” she said. “They’ve lost employees. Their customer base is gone, and they’ve just shuttered.”

At El Mercadito, a long-standing Mexican market with traditional restaurants, clothing stalls and a range of other vendors, shop owners said trepidation surrounding immigration activity has frightened customers away and turned the once busy hallways into a quieter affair.

Leather shoes and belts line the walls of Ricardo Nuñez González’s small shop, but now there seem to be fewer people coming in to buy them. He immigrated here from Sahuayo, in the Mexican state of Michoacán; inherited the store from his mother; and has been working there for more than 30 years.

He says business was down about 80% last June and has since improved, but it’s still not where it used to be. Many potential customers, he said, have turned to online shopping. In other cases, he fears they are preparing for the worst.

“A lot of people, what they do is saving money, like we say in Spanish, just in case,” Nuñez González said. “If we got deported, just in case we’re gonna have some money saved.”

When business is slow, he said he is forced to cut his workers’ hours, but he does not want to let any of them go.

“At least I’m going to try to do my best as long as I can,” he said.

Pressley Has Conducted Oversight of ICE Facilities in MA and Acrossthe Country, Advocated for Children Detained by ICE, Named Impacted Families as Honorary State of the Union Guests

Pressley Has Stood in Vigorous Defense of Immigrant Communities, Fought to Bring Detained Neighbors Home, and Led Efforts to Address Childhood Trauma

Media Availability (YouTube) | Photos (Dropbox)

PLYMOUTH, MA – Today, Congresswoman Ayanna Pressley (MA-07), alongside Congressmen James P. McGovern (MA-02) and Stephen F. Lynch (MA-08), conducted an unannounced Congressional oversight visit of the Plymouth County Correctional Facility—the only facility in Massachusetts currently holding civil immigration detainees on a long-term basis. Federal law gives members of Congress the authority to conduct unannounced oversight visits of ICE detention facilities without providing advance notice.

Following their visit, the lawmakers held a media availability calling for the release of individuals unlawfully imprisoned there and accountability for the harm and trauma caused by Trump and ICE’s campaign of terror. Congresswoman Pressley also called for the release of her constituent Darwin, whose fiancée joined the lawmakers following the visit, and who has suffered from traumatic physical injuries and treatment in prior ICE custody and reported lack of access to health assistive devices, potable water, and nourishing food at the Plymouth facility.

“Under this cruel, lawless Trump administration, families are being separated, children are traumatized, and our communities are suffering,” said Congresswoman Pressley. “I came to Plymouth to conduct an oversight visit of a major detention facility in our state, check on my constituents, and demand accountability of ICE as they deny the humanity and rights of our community members. Learning of the trauma experienced by innocent individuals like my constituent Darwin and his fiancé are a damning reminder of the injustice of these detentions and the need to abolish ICE, end qualified immunity for ICE agents, and stop Trump and ICE’s campaign of terror. Today, I am more resolute than ever in my fight for the freedom, dignity, and humanity of our immigrant neighbors.”

“In 2018, I became the first Member of Congress to demand that we abolish ICE,” said Congressman McGovern. “After hearing heartbreaking stories today at the Plymouth detention facility from folks who were abducted by ICE on their way to work and ripped away from their families, my resolve to abolish ICE has never been stronger. Under orders from the Trump administration, masked federal agents are terrorizing our communities, stalking our streets, and executing American citizens in broad daylight with impunity. Any American with a conscience must join us in calling for this rogue agency to be abolished, for ICE agents to be held accountable, and for the human rights and dignity of immigrants to be respected without condition.”

“While President Trump claims that ICE operations are targeting the “worst of the worst,” the individuals in ICE custody that we met with today included a police officer and construction workers who were on the job with valid work permits and active Social Security numbers. In fact, many of the individuals in ICE detention at the Plymouth Correctional Facility have open immigration cases and prior to their arbitrary arrests, were seeking to comply with the formal processes governing applications for immigrant visas, asylum, and humanitarian parole. Absent substantive reforms including body camera requirements, a prohibition on agents wearing masks, the termination of arbitrary enforcement operations, and the adoption of humane use of force standards, ICE will continue to operate outside the law and we must keep fighting to oppose agency funding,” said Rep. Lynch. “We must also keep exercising our legal right, as Members of Congress, to conduct unannounced oversight inspections of ICE detention facilities to better ensure that individuals in custody are treated humanely and that ICE is transparent and accountable to the American people.”

In Congress, Congresswoman Pressley has been a leading voice in pushing back against Trump, defending our immigrant neighbors, and calling for ICE to be abolished. Rep. Pressley has visited individuals behind the wall at detention facilities in Texas, Louisiana, and Massachusetts and leads legislation to bring accountability to families whose loved ones have been murdered and harmed by ICE agents, including the DHS Use of Force Transparency Act and the Qualified Immunity Abolition Act.

A transcript of Congresswoman Pressley’s remarks is available below and the video from the media availability is available here. Photos from the visit are available here.

Transcript: Rep. Pressley’s Remarks Following Unannounced Oversight Visit of Plymouth ICE Facility

U.S. House of Representatives

August 14, 2026

Well, and let me just, you know—I know technically they are characterized as detainees—but just to center their humanity, today we met with Jose, we met with Alexis, we met with Darwin.

These are sons. These are fathers. These are husbands. Men who are loved by their families, whose labor is valued and essential to the functioning of our communities and our economies. They are sorely missed by their families, and they desperately miss their families.

Jose, for example, 30 years old, has a four-year-old and a two-year-old. He’s never met his two-year-old daughter Ariella—Ariela, rather. And as Jim mentioned, he was a police officer in Ecuador, and in his time spent here, he has worked in construction.

We met with, with Darwin and Alexis, and both talked about how they miss working, and they’re, they’re eager to get back to work. They find dignity in their work, they take pride in their work. They take pride in the role that they play, many of them as the sole breadwinners in their families, not only their families here, but money that they are sending back to countries like Ecuador, Honduras.

I asked about where are most of the detainees from, and the countries were Guatemala, El Salvador, Ecuador, and Honduras, with some rare exceptions.

But what is very clear is that this is a waste of money and a waste of time. And for what? We have separated families. We are causing trauma, and we have people that are providing valuable contributions to community, of which we are all being denied.

So it is a tremendous injustice to these families and a great disservice to our communities writ-large.

One of the, one of the men that we met with, Darwin. This is his fiancé Angelina, and I’m going to turn things over to her in a moment. But I want to say two things.

I’ve said repeatedly that our strategy as a Democratic caucus is litigation, legislation, agitation, when necessary, and mobilization.

The reason we could do this unannounced visit today is because of litigation initiated by our task force, and because that, the court sided with Joe Neguse, Congressman Neguse, and the rest of us who signed on to that—that is why we could do this today.

So, although the work of litigation can move more slowly than we would like, that is why we could do this unannounced visit today.

Secondly, I reinforced for Jose, Alexis, and Darwin that there are people who’ve never met them, who care about them, and are fighting for their freedom. And they all expressed the relief that they felt in knowing that, that they had not been forgotten.

And so, in that aim, I also want to acknowledge that since two of the gentlemen here who were arrested and detained were picked up in Vermont, and so we made sure they knew that Senator Welch and Senator Sanders, that we were here, you know, in their stead, and again that there are people working vigorously on their behalf.

And so I now turn it over to Angelina to tell more of Darwin’s story.

text:
A U.S. soldier's wife who spent more than a month in federal immigration detention said she is back home after officers removed her from a deportation flight to Brazil.

Earlier this month, The Associated Press highlighted Maisa Lopes Eliaser as one of dozens of spouses or parents of U.S. troops who had been detained after President Donald Trump’s administration rolled back protections for military families amid its push for mass deportations. Following the AP’s reporting, a group of Congressional Democrats launched an investigation into deportations of military service members and their families.

Eliaser was placed on a deportation flight Wednesday to her native Brazil when U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers on the plane received a phone call about her mid-flight, she told the AP. She said she was then asked by an ICE officer whether she wanted to continue on to Brazil or go back to the U.S.

RELATED STORY | ICE plans to give officers gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks

“Who made the call? We don’t know,” said Eliaser’s husband, Army Staff Sgt. Alexis Jaramillo. “But someone made the phone call, and then she came back.”

While other detainees were led off the plane in Brazil, Eliaser stayed on board and returned to Louisiana. ICE officers told her that she was “famous” because there were videos about her case, she said.

The U.S. Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

DHS previously told AP that Eliaser, 32, had been issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on April 15, after overstaying the tourist visa she used to enter the U.S. in 2019.

Jaramillo, a 43-year-old aviation operations specialist who has served in the Army for more than a decade, took leave of his duties training soldiers in Fort Polk, Louisiana, to care of Eliaser's 5-year-old son after she was detained on July 8.

Jaramillo said Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, a former Navy officer, also looked into his wife’s case. Kelly’s office didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

RELATED STORY | ICE agent points gun at Virginia woman who shouted at them in video

“This family’s reunion is proof of what’s possible when people set politics aside and do right by those who serve,” said Danitza James, president of the organization Repatriate Our Patriots, which supports military families facing deportation and helped with Eliaser’s case. “We won’t stop until every military family facing detention gets the same chance at justice.”

Eliaser, who was detained in July while at an immigration appointment, has another appointment scheduled for Monday in an effort to reopen her case and advance her green card application. Jaramillo is a U.S. citizen and the couple have been married since 2024.

Jaramillo said he has been told that there will be no further issues with Eliaser’s case, but the couple is still concerned.

“We are really, really, really scared about it, but you know, we have to go,” Jaramillo said. “I told the person who gave me the appointment, ‘Hey sir, don’t play with me, I’ve been through a lot.’”

Eliaser said she is still struggling to sleep and is afraid she will be sent back to the detention facility, where she said she was treated like “an animal.”

“It felt like I was in a nightmare,” Eliaser said. “I could not believe what was happening until I returned to my house. Day by day, I’m trying to recover from this trauma.”

text:
Source:

Media Inquiries: sadaf@muslimadvocates.org, media@haitianbridge.org, media@naacpldf.org

(Boston, M.A.) – On Friday, a federal district court judge in the District of Massachusetts allowed the termination of Somalia’s Temporary Protected Status (TPS) designation to move forward by lifting the administrative stay that temporarily paused the termination of the program while legal arguments were heard in the case.

On July 30, plaintiffs filed an amended complaint arguing that the termination of Somalia’s TPS designation discriminated on the basis of race and national origin. The complaint also contained new claims that the termination violated the due process rights of Somali TPS holders and that the government official who purportedly terminated Somalia’s TPS designation did not have the legal authority to do so.

Although the district court recognized the “undisguised racial animus” inherent in the termination of Somalia’s TPS, the importance of TPS benefits, and the “convincing showing” of irreparable harm, the court felt bound by the U.S. Supreme Court’s June 2026 decision in Mullin v. Doe that greenlit the Trump administration’s discriminatory agenda to terminate TPS for Haiti and Syria.

The Plaintiffs in the lawsuit are African Communities Together (ACT), Partnership for the Advancement of New Americans (PANA), and four Somali community members who have lived and worked in the U.S. for many years and who all have U.S. citizen family members. They now face significant harms from the termination, among them detention, deportation, loss of work authorization, and separation from their family members, loved ones, and communities. The Plaintiffs are represented by Muslim Advocates, Haitian Bridge Alliance, and the Legal Defense Fund, in a lawsuit supported by Communities United for Status and Protection (CUSP).

The Plaintiffs and their legal representatives made the following statement:

“This decision delivers a tremendous blow to the safety of Somali TPS communities all across the nation, opening the door to deportation and violence at the hands of federal agents. We are deeply dismayed at the devastation that will be left in the wake of this ruling but will not stop in our fight to protect the rights of Somali people.”

For those impacted by this decision, we recommend these next steps:

Consult an individual immigration attorney and speak to them as soon as possible about any other pathways to legal status.

Emergency Planning Guide (note: you have to click on the arrow next to “click to download resource” to see the guide)

Temporary Protected Status is a humanitarian protection established by Congress to prevent deportations to countries experiencing armed conflict, environmental disasters, or other extraordinary conditions.

###

Communities United for Status & Protection (CUSP) is a national collaborative of grassroots immigrant-led organizations working to win permanent status for TPS holders and build a more inclusive immigrant rights movement that centers African, Afro-Caribbean, Afro-Latinx, Arab/Middle Eastern, and Asian & Pacific Islander immigrants.

African Communities Together (ACT) is an organization of African immigrants fighting for civil rights, opportunity, and a better life for our families here in the U.S. and worldwide.

text:
Multiple U.S. Immigration Customs and Enforcement agents armed with guns attempted to inspect a Sacramento immigration law firm — and threatened to return later and break windows — on Friday morning, according to several employees of the building.

Employees of the North Natomas law firm and next door dentistry office said the agents, who arrived in at least four vehicles, claimed to have received a list from Washington, D.C., which listed the building’s address as the primary mailing address for many people. The ICE agents requested to tour the office for beds, but were ultimately turned away after failing to provide a warrant.

ICE and the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to questions about the incident.

Under President Donald Trump’s second term, federal immigration officials have used a multitude of unprecedented tactics to crack down on both undocumented immigrants and individuals following the legal pathway. But UC Davis Law Professor Kevin Johnson, an expert on immigration law and civil rights, said he hadn’t heard of agents attempting to enter an immigration law firm and search for beds.

“You might try to collect evidence and information about undocumented people, but you have to have a warrant for that,” Johnson said.

Raissa Morris, owner of the Morris Law Group, received a text at 9:16 a.m. which read “immigration is here.” The message came from one of her employees who told her an agent, who was armed and wearing an ICE badge, had entered the front lobby and asked to speak to an office manager.

She quickly told one of her employees to tell an agent that they could not inspect the building without a warrant. The agent responded by saying that they had received a list from Washington, D.C., which featured multiple clients using the law firm’s address. He asked to inspect the office for beds and said if they received follow-up orders that they could return at 3 a.m. to break windows and enter.

Morris said clients of immigration lawyers, especially victims of crimes, routinely use an office’s address as their mailing address. Her law firm represents more than 2,000 clients.

“I know my rights as an attorney, but I was also afraid for my clients, like the clients that have to come in to pick up notices, pick up mail from us, have appointments throughout the day,” Morris told The Sacramento Bee. “And honestly, I was also afraid for my staff because we know the news — what’s happened in all other places.”

The agents remained for the next hour until Daniel Azurduy, a dentist and the building manager, arrived. Azurduy told the men that, without a warrant, they were trespassing and threatened to call the police. They left shortly after.

“I feel frustrated that there is no transparency with following the law,” Azurduy said. “I believe in the constitution, and I believe that there are rules that people should follow in the proper channels to do the right thing.”

Photos provided to The Bee show at least four unmarked and solidly black vehicles — Chevrolet Tahoe, Dodge Durango, Ford truck and Nissan Pathfinder — in the parking lot of the building. Another photo displays the back of a man, who is not in uniform but wearing a plaid shirt and hat.

Johnson questioned the strategy of agents attempting to enter an immigration law office, given that attorneys are more knowledgeable of the law compared to the average person.

“Any immigration attorney is going to say no way,” Johnson said. “So it’s like a waste of time.”

text:
The front- and rear-facing dashboard cameras that Carolina Molina has mounted on her Toyota Supra are, by her telling, for accountability.

“It’s for traffic incidents. I have a nice car, and if somebody were to hit me I want proof of that,” she said. “You just never know what could happen, so you should always protect yourself.”

But earlier this week, the dashcams became a tool for a different type of accountability.

On Monday, a masked ICE agent confronted Molina as she drove through an office park in the Bailey’s Crossroads area of Northern Virginia, pointing a gun at her head while accusing her of trying to run them over. She says he was lying, and had the dashcam footage to prove it.

Trending

Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Molina — a first-generation American whose family is from El Salvador — caught the rest of the interaction with her cellphone’s camera, and she posted the footage on Instagram.

The footage immediately went viral, prompting widespread criticism over the agent’s aggressive tactics and again pointing a spotlight at ICE, which came under intense scrutiny earlier this year for two killings in Minnesota and again this summer for similar fatalities in Texas and Maine.

The Department of Homeland Security is standing by the agents involved, accusing Molina in a statement of “weaponizing her vehicle against them — all in an attempt to help illegal aliens get away.” The agency also said Molina herself “could face criminal prosecution as a result of her actions.”

Democratic Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, who represents Virginia’s 10th Congressional District, is calling for criminal charges to be pressed against the agent, not Molina.

“They have no right to attack someone who exercises their First Amendment right to free speech,” he told NOTUS. “If ICE doesn’t want to have people jeer [at] them wherever they go, they should change their tactics. They should be more accountable, more transparent to the American people.”

But Patrick Jaicomo, an attorney specializing in police conduct for the libertarian Institute for Justice, says that accountability may be hard to come by.

“When you see federal agents violating someone’s rights, there should be an avenue to seek relief in court,” he says. “But there is very little to be done, and we’ve had to piece together novel theories to restore some avenue for federal accountability. The federal government has no interest in holding itself accountable no matter how egregious the behavior is.”

After ICE agents fatally shot two people in Minnesota in January, the uproar prompted DHS leaders to promise to outfit agents nationwide with body cameras, which advocates tout as one tool to ensure that there’s a record of when things go wrong. While that rollout hasn’t been completed, the agents who confronted Molina were wearing body cameras.

But whether the footage is released remains an open question. The Associated Press recently reported that the agency’s existing policy gives it full discretion over whether to release footage from body cameras, and specifies it will do so when “it is in the best interests of the agency.”

This conflicts with policies in many local law enforcement agencies, including D.C.’s Metropolitan Police Department, which mandate that footage showing a serious use of force be made public within five days of the incident — unless the victim or their family objects. (Earlier this year, the D.C. Council passed a bill expanding the release of footage to include situations where federal agents use serious force when patrolling with D.C. police officers. A group of Republican senators is now trying to repeal that law.)

An email to a DHS spokesperson inquiring as to whether the footage in Molina’s case would be released went unanswered. Molina said Wednesday she would like to see it made public, and Subramanyam said he plans to request the footage from DHS — but also that the agency’s existing policy troubles him.

“That policy makes clear that they don’t care about the American people; they only care about themselves and protecting the administration and its immigration overreach,” he said. “If they cared about our country and the American people, they would release body camera footage and all the other information related to an incident like this, so that everyone knew what was going on and exactly what happened, and we could fix the issue.”

Molina conceded that had she not been equipped to record the interaction, things could have ended much worse for her.

“I think they would have shot me and gotten away with it,” she said.

“Body cameras are a good thing,” Jaicomo said. “They are used in many cases to show the objective truth of what happened. They can show a criminal did criminal things or the police lied. In this case, it’s the latter. But if those videos are never recorded or made public, they serve no purpose.”

Another element of Molina’s incident was that the ICE agents were masked — as they have been through much of the Trump administration. Earlier this year, Virginia lawmakers approved a bill prohibiting federal agents from being masked, but it is currently held up in litigation. Democratic Virginia Sens. Mark Warner and Tim Kaine have introduced legislation to end masking by federal agents.

“There must be an increase in transparency, accountability, and safety in immigration law enforcement,” Warner said in an email to NOTUS. “My Immigration Enforcement Identification Act would make it illegal for law enforcement officers to obscure their faces and require that they clearly display their agency, name, and a unique identifier while conducting immigration enforcement functions. It also has some commonsense exceptions for select tactical missions and officer health and safety.”

For Subramanyam, Monday’s incident shows why some people want to scrap ICE altogether, he said. But he wouldn’t go that far.

“We do need to do immigration reform, but not like this. We do need to do immigration enforcement, but not like this,” he said. “What we need is a completely new way of doing immigration enforcement.”

As for Molina, a therapist by trade, she said she isn’t yet sure how she’ll proceed but that she will be speaking to an attorney. She wants the ICE agents who confronted her to be investigated, but absent that, she proposed her own form of accountability: “therapy.”

text:
In a final rule released Aug. 10, 2026, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced that employers with at least 50 U.S. employees, with more than half of whom holding H-1B, L-1A or L-1B status, must pay the Biometric Fee, $4,000 for an H-1B petition or $4,500 for an L-1 petition, for all extension-of-status petitions. Amended petitions that do not request an extension remain exempt. The rule goes into effect on Sept. 9, 2026.

Until now, DHS generally collected the fee when a covered employer first sponsored a worker or filed a change-of-employer petition but not for an extension petition. The agency said that approach improperly tied the biometric fee to a separate fraud-prevention fee. According to DHS, Congress signaled in the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2016 that the biometric fee also applies to extensions of status.

DHS reported that only 27% of H-1B petitions filed by covered employers between fiscal years 2018 and 2025 were charged the fee. Had the new interpretation applied during that period, approximately 75% would have been subject to the fee. DHS did not provide a comparable calculation for L-1 petitions.

Employers, particularly smaller businesses, raised cost concerns during the rulemaking process. DHS received 146 public comments and estimated that, at most, about 16% of small businesses filing H-1B or L-1 petitions could be affected. The agency acknowledged the added burden but added that the result reflects the best reading of the statute and Congress’ intent.

DHS also said the added collections are needed to implement and maintain its biometric entry-exit system, which is designed to strengthen security and detect fraudulent travel documents. It expects the rule to generate an additional $37.9 million in fiscal year 2026 and $40 million in fiscal year 2027.

Under previous congressional action (Public Law 114–113), the Biometric Fee applies to qualifying petitions filed on or before Sept. 30, 2027.

Covered employers should review upcoming extension-of-status filings now and account for the additional cost in their budgets.

text:
By The New Bedford Light via The Associated Press

The Plymouth County Sheriff’s Office must hand over hundreds of anonymized health records of immigrant detainees following a Massachusetts court ruling.

Judge James Budreau issued the order, released Wednesday, a month after attorneys for the sheriff and the American Civil Liberties Union of Massachusetts sparred in Suffolk County Superior Court.

“I think this is a decision that is important for government transparency and the rights of immigrant detainees,” said Dan McFadden, managing attorney at the state ACLU. “(The Sheriff’s Office) cannot exempt itself from public records law simply by contract with ICE.”

Karen Barry, spokeswoman for the Sheriff’s Office, told The Light in an email that the office will comply with the order.

“As the judge acknowledged, this is a novel case,” she said. “We appreciate the court’s guidance.”

The ACLU sued for numerous records generated for immigrant detainees at Plymouth County Correctional Facility, the only immigrant detention facility in Massachusetts. That stems from a contract the department signed with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in 2024. The ACLU sued after the Sheriff’s Office denied a public records request.

At the July 7 hearing, the Sheriff’s Office relied largely on legal concepts of pre-emption — arguing that federal law prohibited them from issuing the health records. The sheriff’s attorneys argued that federal dominion over immigration law pre-empted the state’s public records law in this case, despite the Sheriff’s Office being a state agency.

Budreau brushed that concern aside in his decision.

“The state law at issue is not, however, an attempt by the Commonwealth to regulate the documentation of immigrants,” he said. “Rather, the question before this court is about the state maintaining records relating to the state’s police powers and oversight of the health and safety of persons held in state facilities.

“The state maintains (its) right to reasonably police and ensure the health and safety of its population,” he went on to say, “and such right is not usurped by the federal regulation at issue here.”

The ACLU had filed a motion for summary judgment to compel the handover of the documents in response to the sheriff’s motion for dismissal. Budreau said the judgment will be entered within 30 days should neither party request a hearing on that motion.

The July hearing

The ACLU argued in court on July 7 that the laws the sheriff cited in its denial of the records were overly broad, and that the sheriff was attempting to circumvent state law.

“It would be pretty extraordinary if Congress tried to interfere in state agencies’ abilities to generate its own record,” McFadden said.

Jessica Kenny, the sheriff department’s attorney, argued that the ACLU could attempt to procure the documents through a federal Freedom of Information Act request to ICE.

“These documents were created pursuant to the (ICE-sheriff agreement), so ICE does have the records,” she said.

When Budreau pressed Kenny on whether the redaction of detainees’ names, alien registration numbers, and any other identifying information could resolve the issue, she quickly assented.

“If those are redacted, there’s no way of connecting that to a detainee?” Budreau asked.

“Presumably no,” Kenny responded.

History of issues

Plymouth County Correctional Facility began to house immigrant detainees through a contract with the now defunct-Immigration and Naturalization Service in 1998. It is currently the only such facility to house immigrant detainees long term in Massachusetts.

According to its contract with ICE, Plymouth sets aside 250 beds at the facility for immigrant detainees. The agency pays the Sheriff’s Office $215 per day per occupied bed.

The contract also obligates the Sheriff’s Office to create the health records. The ACLU filed its initial records request seeking those records on Dec. 11.

“The availability of medical care in immigration detention facilities is vitally important, as immigration detainees have no other way to seek medical help while detained,” wrote Mackenzie Saunders, an ACLU attorney, in the original complaint. “And for some, not receiving medical care can be a matter of life or death.”

A 2024 report published by the Boston University School of Law and Prisoners’ Legal Services of Massachusetts found through interviews with detainees that Plymouth authorities did not provide detainees with necessary care and services. It recommended the sheriff ensure inmates had timely access to necessary medical care and to discontinue the use of solitary confinement. Another 2024 report by the ICE Office of Detention Oversight found the prison had “no deficiencies” in treatment.

As of Aug. 4, 57 people had died in ICE custody nationwide since Donald Trump’s return to the presidency, according to the National Immigration Project. The ACLU cited the fatalities, and other reports of ill-treatment, in its complaint.

Several of those detainees died of what may appear to be minor problems. On March 2, 56-year old Emmanuel Damas, a Haitian man living in Boston, died at a hospital in Scottsdale, Arizona, while in custody from an untreated tooth infection.

text:
More than 20,000 migrant children nationwide could end up representing themselves in immigration court after the Trump administration allowed a federal contract that funded their attorneys to expire last month.

Without legal representation these children, many of whom are fleeing from abuse and trafficking in their home countries, will almost certainly be deported, according to immigration lawyers who specialize in unaccompanied child cases.

“Our analysis has shown that (children) are 99% likely to be ordered deported if (they) go to court without a lawyer,” said Bilal Askaryar, director of communications with the Acacia Center for Justice.

Acacia is the umbrella organization that, until July 31, received a $356 million contract from the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to provide legal representation to unaccompanied immigrant children. The nonprofit distributed those funds to more than 100 legal aid organizations throughout the country.

Without that federal funding, some of those organizations are shutting down their unaccompanied children work, Askaryar said.

2-year-olds representing themselves

The federal government began paying for the legal representation of unaccompanied migrant children in 2008, after lawmakers passed the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act. That law requires the federal government to represent children who crossed the border alone out of concern that they could be easily exploited, abused or trafficked.

Since then, the work has been contracted out to small nonprofits and legal clinics that specialize in working with immigrants and children.

“We’ve seen clients as young as 2 years old,” said Monica Valencia, managing attorney with Al Otro Lado, a San Diego-based non-profit that received federal funding through Acacia.

Immigration lawyers who work with children — particularly children who have been abused — often have to play the role of social worker and therapist.

It’s not uncommon for lawyers to bring teddy bears to their first meeting with a new child client. Or use toy models of courtrooms to prepare children for a court appearance.

“To ask them to represent themselves in court is just completely absurd,” Valencia said.

'Not political pawns'

The expiration of Acacia's federal contact comes after a long-running battle with the Trump administration.

It began in April 2025 when the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) sent Acacia a stop work order. The conflict escalated in November 2025 when the Trump administration stopped paying Acacia invoices for work Al Otro Lado and dozens of other subcontractors had already performed.

The government’s lawyers argued in court that HHS withheld funding because Acacia refused to hand over information about their clients. Acacia said releasing personal information would violate attorney-client privilege.

Providers like Valencia say it feels like children are collateral damage in a political fight.

“Children are not political pawns,” she said. “They’re not line items in a procurement process and they should not pay the price for political agendas.”

Contracts to Trump-aligned groups?

Immigration lawyers expressed concern over reports that the federal government could continue the funding by awarding child representation contracts to law firms that have connections to the Trump administration, but have little immigration law experience.

“Instead of investing in the experienced non-profit network that has spent years protecting vulnerable children, the Trump administration is using its political accomplices to gamble with the futures of children,” Valencia said.

One of the firms, Texas-based Burke Law Group, was founded by Marcella Burke who served as a lawyer for the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and the Department of the Interior during President Trump’s first term.

Burke Law Group has since declined the contract.

Another group under consideration is the Minneapolis-based nonprofit Our Rescue, which was founded by a former Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent who was appointed co-chair of a group that made anti-trafficking recommendations to the White House in 2019.

Our Rescue founder Tim Ballard left the organization in 2023 after five women filed a lawsuit alleging he coerced them into sexual acts. Ballard was also accused of sex trafficking and forced labor in a 2024 federal lawsuit that is ongoing.

“It calls into question what kind of country we want to be,” said Askaryar of Acacia. “When a child comes to our door alone or abandoned, neglected, trafficked and asks us of help, do we want to give them a lawyer who knows how to talk to them in a child-friendly way, or do we want to give them over to an organization that is just going to be a rubber stamp to deport them as quickly as possible?”

text:
The Trump administration has largely ended a pathway to citizenship for DACA recipients who marry U.S. citizens.

President Trump tried, unsuccessfully, to end DACA during his first term. This week’s action reflects his administration’s ongoing focus on the Obama-era program that shields from deportation hundreds of thousands of immigrants, often referred to as Dreamers, who were brought to the U.S. as children.

“It was inevitable that what Trump was going to do in office this time was to embark on a massive delegalization mission,” said Karen Tumlin, director of the Justice Action Center in Los Angeles. “That’s what this is.”

Tumlin was referring to a ruling by an administrative immigration court that was published Thursday.

The ruling concerns a travel provision afforded to recipients of Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals, the program created in 2012. The provision allows DACA recipients to travel in ways other people without legal status cannot.

DACA isn’t technically a form of legal status, though its recipients are granted work permits.

For immigrants who entered the U.S. illegally, leaving the country or being deported triggers a penalty — many are banned from coming back into the U.S. for a decade.

Most people who qualify for legal residency, or a green card, have to serve that 10-year ban before they can apply for the green card, which can lead to citizenship.

But DACA recipients, under the travel provision called advance parole, could leave the U.S. for school, work or humanitarian reasons. When they returned through an airport or border, the stain of their original unlawful entry was erased.

With the penalty wiped away, a DACA recipient married to a U.S. citizen or who had another way to obtain legal residency could start that process for a green card without delay.

Thursday’s ruling by the Board of Immigration Appeals does away with that benefit.

U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services spokesman Zach Kahler said the decision confirms a “straightforward principle” that departing the U.S. has meaning.

“The immigration laws enacted by Congress impose consequences when someone who has accrued unlawful presence leaves the country and later seeks admission, including when that departure occurs under advance parole,” he said. “U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services will ensure that immigration filings are decided based on the laws, regulations, and binding legal precedent that govern each case.”

Immigration attorneys and other advocates quickly convened Thursday to determine how the ruling will affect immigrants.

Tumlin said some DACA recipients can still safely travel with advance parole, while for others — particularly those with deportation orders — it would be too risky to leave. She said DACA recipients should consult an immigration attorney before traveling.

“For over a decade, I could reassure my clients that traveling on Advance Parole was a safe option,” Shilpa Malik, an immigration lawyer in Florida, wrote Thursday on X. “What was once a vital protection is now gone.”

Under the ruling, having the travel document may no longer protect certain DACA recipients when they return from their trips abroad, because leaving could expose them to the years-long ban.

The decision also makes obtaining green cards more difficult. Tumlin said some DACA recipients could qualify for waivers that allow them to avoid the years-long reentry ban, but the waivers are granted under limited circumstances.

The latest federal data show there are 455,000 DACA recipients in the U.S. as of March, with about 126,000 in California.

According to the nonpartisan Congressional Research Service, 45,447 DACA recipients were approved for advance parole as of Aug. 21, 2017.

About 76,000 DACA recipients had become legal residents as of July 31, 2019, most after marrying a U.S. citizen, according to the research service. It’s unclear how many DACA recipients have obtained advance parole or green cards since then.

Path2Papers, a project at Cornell Law School, analyzed 1,600 consults and estimated that around 60% of DACA recipients would be subject to the 10-year ban.

Republicans have viewed advance parole as an abuse of the immigration system.

The office of Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) blasted the provision, saying in 2017 that “the Obama administration allowed thousands of DACA recipients to exploit an immigration law loophole to obtain green cards.”

Last year, Grassley introduced a bill to guarantee that it would no longer be used by immigrants seeking to adjust their legal status. This week’s ruling essentially accomplishes that goal.

The immigration appeals board’s decision applies to future travel. People who previously traveled and returned to the U.S. won’t be affected and could still adjust their immigration status.

Tumlin said Thursday’s decision is yet another effort to change the goalposts for DACA recipients by an administration that has resorted to ending the program “through death by a thousand cuts.”

The Department of Homeland Security has arrested hundreds of immigrants with DACA, and in a February letter to U.S. senators, then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem said the agency had deported 86 DACA recipients between Jan. 1 and Nov. 19, 2025.

text:
The U.S. strikes on several fishing boats near Ecuador’s Galápagos Islands earlier this year were part of a secret operation conducted by the Central Intelligence Agency, the CIA. That’s according to The Washington Post, which spoke to a source anonymously. One of the boats disappeared on January 20 along with eight of its crew members, who are presumed dead, according to the United Nations. Survivors of two other vessels that came under attack in March said they were abducted by U.S. forces, hooded, cuffed and tortured aboard a ship before being taken to El Salvador. No U.S. government agency has claimed responsibility for those strikes, which the Post reports are separate from the Trump administration’s publicly acknowledged strikes on boats off the Caribbean and Pacific. The Pentagon has provided no evidence for its claims the boats were carrying drugs. More than 200 people have been killed in the U.S. strikes since September.

Meanwhile, U.S. Southern Command and Panama have concluded PANAMAX 2026, a series of war games involving at least 17 other countries from across the Americas. It was the first time joint U.S. military exercises took place in Panama since 2012.

In Gaza, Israeli attacks killed two Palestinians and injured several others on Thursday, with reports of airstrikes, mortar attacks and live fire. The strikes came as human rights groups warned Israel is conducting a massive effort to clear tens of thousands of tons of rubble from the Gaza Strip. The debris resulted from Israel’s near-daily attacks on Gaza since October 2023, which have killed at least 73,000 Palestinians. Some of the rubble is from cemeteries and other locations where human remains are known to exist, leading human rights groups to accuse Israel of attempting to erase evidence of war crimes.

Iran’s military has rejected the Trump administration’s claims that ships are freely passing through the Strait of Hormuz, saying no one can pass without Iran’s permission.

This comes as the Pentagon has announced it will send a new aircraft carrier to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln amid reports of deteriorating conditions aboard the vessel. The USS George Washington is set to relieve the Lincoln, which has been deployed for over eight months. On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth dismissed reports in Stars and Stripes and the Military Times about a growing mental health crisis aboard the Lincoln, where sailors face moldy showers, backed-up plumbing and shortages of nutritious food, toiletries and other supplies. Despite Hegseth’s denials, a U.S. official confirmed that a sailor jumped overboard from the Lincoln in early August, saying the person was quickly rescued. The sailor had missed the birth of his daughter five months ago and reportedly complained to his higher-ups about mental health challenges before attempting suicide. On Thursday, the Senate Veterans’ Affairs Committee’s top Democrat, Richard Blumenthal, demanded answers about problems aboard the Lincoln.

The New York Times reports the Trump administration carried out an expansive surveillance program targeting left-leaning groups in Minnesota, infiltrating group chats, spying on meetings at libraries and churches and secretly obtaining financial records of organizations that were never accused of crimes. Among groups targeted were labor unions, including the Communications Workers of America, the SEIU and the AFL-CIO, and climate activists with the Sunrise Movement. The massive spying operation began last winter as hundreds of thousands of Minnesotans joined protests demanding an end to a violent mass deportation campaign by ICE and other federal agencies. Government documents reveal DHS characterized the protesters as “violent opportunists and agitators,” alleging they were involved in a widespread conspiracy. The surveillance operation arose from a White House directive known as National Security Presidential Memo 7, which identifies a potential domestic terrorist as someone expressing “anti-Christian,” “anti-capitalism” or “anti-American” views. The civil liberties advocacy group Defending Rights and Dissent called the surveillance “a disturbing, invasive, and utterly unjustifiable attack on freedom of expression and political dissent.” Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen responded, “These are the actions of an authoritarian state.”

In Texas, bulldozers have rolled into Big Bend National Park to tear down portions of the environmental landmark as part of the Trump administration’s $46.5 billion effort to expand a massive border wall and other security infrastructure along the border with Mexico. Protesters gathered Thursday at Big Bend seeking to block construction of the wall, after the Department of Homeland Security waived requirements that federal contractors comply with a broad slate of environmental laws, including the Endangered Species Act.

Meanwhile, in southern Arizona, a protest camp predominantly led by queer and femme activists in the small border town of Lochiel is seeking to protect ancient cottonwood trees, as federal contractors race to build another portion of Trump’s border barrier with Mexico at a cost of about a half a billion dollars. At the center of the protest camp is a 200-year-old cottonwood known as a “grandmother” tree.

Ukraine has proposed a deal with Russia that would see both sides halt attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea. Reuters reports the offer came as part of an effort to reopen a crucial grain corridor amid warnings that the attacks are driving up global food prices, which are already at their highest levels since early 2023. The United Nations reports more civilians were killed or injured in Ukraine in July than in any month since Russia’s full-scale invasion, with at least 437 deaths and over 2,600 injuries in Ukraine in July.

Poland’s prime minister says authorities have arrested a Russian national who was preparing to assassinate a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw. Donald Tusk called it Russia’s first attempted attack on a U.S. citizen in a NATO country.

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Thursday blasted Vladimir Putin over the Russian president’s first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril Islands. It’s one of four islands claimed by both Russia and Japan.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi: “This latest visit to Iturup by the incumbent president of Russia runs contrary to Japan’s consistent position regarding the Northern Territories. Furthermore, it hurts the feelings of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable.”

Meanwhile, President Trump shared a video on Instagram Thursday showing former U.S. Marine Robert Gilman aboard a plane with Trump’s special envoy Steve Witkoff, following Gilman’s release from Russian custody. He had been jailed by Russia for over four years.

The Congressional Black Caucus is calling on the Department of Justice to investigate the mysterious death of Nolan Wells, an 18-year-old Black college athlete whose body was found in July on a barrier island in Mississippi. Wells vanished after taking a boat to the island with a group of white friends over the July Fourth holiday. His body was recovered several days later. Authorities say Wells may have accidentally drowned, but his family has questioned the official story, in part because Wells’s cellphone was found not with his body, but in the possession of one of his friends, who returned home. This is Georgia Democratic Congressmember Lucy McBath.

Rep. Lucy McBath: “This brings back so many vivid memories for me and my own family, having lost Jordan to unnecessary gun violence in November 2012, Black Friday, simply because he was Black and playing loud music in his car. And so, here we are again today, here for the loss of another Black young man in our community, and we find ourselves asking the same questions.”

In Washington, D.C., the board of directors for the Kennedy Center has voted to once again inscribe Donald Trump’s name on the building — and to shutter it for two years, allegedly to make renovations to the performing arts institution. Thursday’s vote by Trump’s hand-picked board comes despite a federal judge’s order barring closure of the Kennedy Center and ordering the Trump administration to remove Trump’s name from the building.

Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are seeking an audit of spending on the White House East Wing and ballroom, after The Washington Post reported the Trump administration plans to spend at least $900 million on new construction. When Trump announced his plans to build a ballroom last year, he repeatedly promised the project would be funded entirely by private donors.

authors: Katie Guenthner, Isabella Volmert, Staff Writers

text:
Zoya Choudhry doesn’t sit still. The 30-year-old activist spends her summer days dashing around in an orange vest emblazoned with a butterfly on the front and back — the symbol of migrants.

Choudhry volunteers with La Colectiva North Texas, a grassroots group that aids people who have appointments at Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s Dallas field office. They tackle logistical challenges, but also provide an emotional and spiritual anchor for people on one of the most difficult days of their lives.

La Colectiva may not be able to stop someone from being deported, Choudhry said. But the volunteers can help detainees’ relatives pay rent and make sure their car doesn’t get towed. Sometimes, even just a bottle of water can make a difference.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

“It’s not charity, it’s empathy,” Choudhry said. “You’re my neighbor and I care about you.”

La Colectiva — which means “the collective” — sets up shop at 5:30 a.m., Mondays through Fridays, with a later start on Saturdays. Volunteers offer snacks, activity kits for children and what people want most — information.

They perch in a tent near the entrance to the Dallas field office, a building off N. Stemmons Freeway that’s a work space for ICE employees, a place for immigrants to complete their regular check-ins, and a location to process detainees who have just been arrested or are being transferred. Some people coming for check-ins are detained there.

“ICE remains committed to ensuring that individuals in custody are treated humanely and that family members and other members of the public are provided appropriate, general information about available processes,” said Sarah Loicano, a spokesperson for ICE’s Dallas field office.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Loicano said when a person is taken into ICE custody, they are generally given the chance to make a phone call. She said ICE personnel also provide information about the detention process, including how relatives may locate an individual through ICE’s online system.

“If an individual is accompanied by family members or others at the field office, officers may provide general information about the detention process at that time,” Loicano said.

At 8:57 a.m. on a recent Friday, Choudhry stopped one woman wearing loose brown pants and a clean white top on her way into her appointment. Choudhry handed her a Department of Homeland Security privacy waiver to write identifying details such as her full name and alien registration number. The waiver allows third parties, such as family members or La Colectiva volunteers, to access information about a detainee.

Choudhry encouraged her to give the waiver to a loved one in case ICE detained her. Without that information, officials may not be able to provide information about her.

“Up until this point, you’ve been robbed of your agency, you’ve been robbed of your choice,” she said. “But what I can do is help them.”

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

The volunteers try to identify patterns in how people are detained, but it’s difficult, she said. It’s not as hard as preparing people for the possibility that they or their loved ones might not walk out after they go for their appointment, though.

“It’s kind of like death,” Choudhry said.

A New York Times analysis found the Dallas field office recorded the second-highest number of immigration arrests — an average of 85 per day — after Miami among ICE field offices nationwide from January 2025 through early March 2026. The Dallas ICE field office covers North Texas and Oklahoma.

A Dallas Morning News analysis found that in 2025, the majority of people arrested by ICE officers in the Dallas area did not have criminal convictions.

Related: As ICE flights pass through Love Field, Dallas says it has no authority over operations

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Rain, snow and shine, the tent is staffed

Around 75 volunteers are involved in three-hour shifts to staff the tent. Many of the volunteers are women, and are known to some as “the ladies of the tent.”

The tent is set up in an abandoned driveway near the pedestrian entrance to the field office. Security has increased at the office after a sniper shot three people detained by ICE, two fatally, last year.

Volunteers on Friday set up netting around the tent’s poles to block the sun and placed battery powered fans to blow into it. But the volunteers were rarely in the tent. The nine who rotated through spent a great deal of time flagging approaching cars, telling the drivers in Spanish that the field office’s parking lot is now for staff personnel only. Yard signs put up by La Colectiva in the sidewalk median directed drivers to an abandoned lot nearby.

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Loicano said the growing number of employees at the office has created a need for more staff parking. She said signs at the field office’s lot say overnight vehicles will be towed.

Two sisters aged 21 and 28 approached the tent around 11 a.m., and Choudhry directed them to sit in lawn chairs in the shade as she crouched to speak with them. The sisters said they dropped off their mother for her appointment around 6 a.m. and she was detained two hours later.

Choudhry explained how to use ICE’s online locator to track where their mother was being held. Some migrants are moved around the state or country before they are deported. The sisters sat very still as they took in the information, interrupting only to ask the occasional question.

By the time the sisters left, it was 95 degrees.

Related: Bulldozers clearing land in Texas’ Big Bend National Park for roads, border barriers

Advertisement

Article continues below this ad

Big and small support

La Colectiva is one of many grassroots organizations that popped up across the country in the wake of increased immigration enforcement. While some groups like El Refugio in Georgia give families of detainees a place to stay outside of detention centers, La Colectiva focuses on helping people in the moments before and after their appointments with ICE.

Sandra Avalos, 37, started the effort in October after seeing a gap of assistance for the people who don’t know how the process works.

Occasionally, La Colectiva has helped cover a month's rent, especially after a family’s breadwinner is detained or deported. The group has helped fund self-deportation flights for those seeking to join their relatives, organizers said.

It’s disheartening at times, Avalos said, to hear children defend their parents, saying their parents are hard working and a good mom or dad. But there are moments that uplift her.

“One of the things that happens a lot is they give us a hug,” she said. “It seems so simple, but someone says ‘This makes a difference. Just connection and to see that you value my humanity.’”

Related: One year later, a weekly vigil for migrants persists in prayer

The work takes a toll

A group of clergy rotate in shifts each day as well, usually adorned with a collar, vestment or neon vest with the word “clergy.”

George Mason, an interfaith leader and one of the clergy on duty Friday, asked a young woman who came out of the office how it went. She responded positively and they embraced. “People need to know they are being seen,” Mason said.

Choudhry, who is the daughter of immigrants, said she feels like she has to volunteer because she knows what it’s like to be afraid of immigration enforcement.

“It is crushing,” Choudhry said. “But I think not being here would kill me more.”

Earlier that morning, shortly after 10:30 a.m., one woman came who didn’t have an appointment. A permanent resident, she came to learn as much as she could before her daughter’s upcoming appointment.

“How good that you came before,” Choudhry told the mother in Spanish.

“They’re very strong in the streets,” the mother said of ICE’s immigration enforcement efforts. “It makes me nervous.”

Choudhry said it’s best to be prepared for any outcome.

The mother left, clutching pamphlets in hand. She thanked Choudhry, because her daughter was too afraid to come.

When the Supreme Court ruled in June that most temporary protected status terminations were beyond judicial review, the decision affected more than 356,000 Haitians and Syrians, and approximately 1.3 million individuals under temporary protected status.
It establishes a rigorous process — including background checks and work, education or military requirements — before recipients can earn permanent status.
